### Related literature {#sec-literature}

This paper sits at the intersection of real options, strategic investment, structural credit risk, and the economics of AI. I organize the review around the four building blocks and then state the marginal contribution.

**Real options and capacity choice.**
The foundation rests on @mcdonald1986value for optimal timing of irreversible investment and @pindyck1988irreversible for capacity choice.^[Other foundational contributions include @brennan1985evaluating and @bernanke1983irreversibility.] @guo2005investment model demand with regime-dependent drift and volatility, showing large investment jumps upon favorable regime arrival; @decamps2006irreversible study irreversible investment with alternative projects under regime switching, using a two-regime structure with an absorbing state that is close to the present paper's $L \to H$ transition. The key difference is that their framework does not include strategic interaction, training-inference allocation, or default risk.^[@bloom2009impact develops time-varying volatility shocks; @jovanovic2005general document S-curve diffusion for general-purpose technologies.]
The capacity-choice side of the problem is also the subject of a large operations management literature, surveyed by @vanmieghem2003capacity, which studies how much capacity to install under demand uncertainty and how flexible that capacity should be.
The closest construct there is resource flexibility: @chod2005resource show that a flexible resource allocated across products *after* demand is observed substitutes for capacity and interacts with pricing.
Compute is flexible in exactly this sense---the same GPU cluster can train or serve---but the allocation here is a commitment made at installation whose training component pays off only in a different demand regime, and it is priced jointly with the firm's default decision rather than taken as an operational problem for a solvent firm.

**Strategic investment.**
@grenadier2002option shows that competition drastically erodes the option value of waiting.^[See also @weeds2002strategic on R\&D delay and @fudenberg1985preemption for game-theoretic foundations.] @huisman2015strategic is the closest strategic investment paper: they study a duopoly with joint timing and capacity choice. I extend their framework with endogenous default risk, training-inference allocation, diminishing returns, and regime switching. @aguerrevere2003equilibrium studies equilibrium incremental capacity investment in oligopoly with time-to-build and the option to idle capacity, showing that operating flexibility can make firms *expand* in response to greater uncertainty; @aguerrevere2009real draws out the asset-pricing implication that installed capacity and competitive intensity jointly determine the composition of firm value between assets in place and growth options, and hence expected returns. That mapping from capacity to risk exposure is the antecedent of the training-beta prediction in @sec-discussion, with the difference that here the risk composition is shifted by the *split* of a given capacity rather than by its level. @lambrecht2003real study real options in duopoly with incomplete information, where firms have private signals about the investment payoff; their setting is related to the present paper's heterogeneous beliefs about the AGI arrival rate $\lambda$---the Poisson intensity of the switch to the high-demand regime, formalized in @sec-model---but they do not model the training-inference allocation or the endogenous default mechanism that links beliefs to survival. The present paper's emphasis on heterogeneous beliefs about $\lambda$ as a driver of cross-sectional variation connects to the broader literature on disagreement and speculation [@harrison1978speculative; @scheinkman2003overconfidence], though here disagreement operates through comparative statics in $\lambda$ rather than through equilibrium trading under heterogeneous priors. @grenadier2011real develop real options signaling games in which investment timing conveys private information---relevant to the future direction of dynamic belief updating about $\lambda$ discussed in @sec-conclusion. @bouis2009multistage provide an $N$-firm sequential entry framework that could extend the duopoly analysis.

**R&D races and arms race dynamics.**
The investment dynamics in this paper also connect to the literature on patent races and R&D competition.
@loury1979market models firms choosing R&D intensity to accelerate a stochastic Poisson breakthrough, showing that competition leads to socially excessive duplication of effort.
@reinganum1982strategic extends the framework to asymmetric firms, demonstrating that the frontrunner invests more aggressively---analogous to the leader's earlier entry in the preemption equilibrium of Proposition 3.
@harris1987racing model R&D as a race with position-dependent investment incentives, producing a "discouragement effect" for lagging firms that echoes the follower's delayed entry in the duopoly equilibrium; notably, in the present model the *allocation* margin is immune to this discouragement (Proposition 3(ii))---position affects when firms invest, not how they split capacity.
@grossman1986optimal study simultaneous timing and scale choices in R&D competition under uncertainty, combining elements of the capacity and timing decisions modeled here.
The key departure from this literature is the dual role of capacity: in standard R&D races, investment during the race is pure cost with no concurrent revenue, whereas here, installed capacity generates inference revenue pre-AGI and training quality determines competitive position post-AGI, creating the allocation trade-off that is absent from existing race models.

**Structural credit risk and investment-financing interactions.**
The default mechanism builds on @merton1974pricing and @leland1994corporate.^[@blackcox1976valuing extend to a first-passage setting.] A well-developed branch of this literature already embeds regime switching in the Leland framework. @hackbarth2006capital let cash flows depend on a two-state macroeconomic regime and derive default and financing policies that adapt to the cycle, reproducing countercyclical leverage ratios and strictly positive short-maturity credit spreads; @chen2010macroeconomic and @bhamra2010levered add a consumption-based pricing kernel, so that risk prices, leverage, and regime-contingent default boundaries are determined jointly. Proposition 2 is therefore not the first default boundary derived in a regime-switching environment; those papers in fact solve the fully coupled system with regime-contingent boundaries, whereas @eq-default-boundary uses a single boundary that embeds the switch in unconditional expectation (@sec-model documents the resulting approximation error). What they do not contain is an intensive margin *inside* the firm's installed capital: in their models the regime governs the cash-flow process exogenously, so the growth option's size is not a decision variable and cannot be traded off against current cash flow. Here the firm chooses $\phi$, and that choice determines both the H-regime continuation value and the L-regime coupon coverage---which is exactly why the default boundary can be *decreasing* in training intensity (@eq-phi-underbar). Put differently, the regime-switching credit literature makes the default boundary depend on the state; the present model makes it depend on how the firm has positioned itself for the state it is waiting for. The most closely related papers combining investment and default are @hackbarth2014capital (real options with endogenous default and product market competition) and @kumar2018optimal (joint leverage and irreversible capacity choice, showing they are substitutes).^[@sundaresan2015dynamic model growth options with default risk; @bolton2019investment model financial constraints on investment.] The present model integrates endogenous default into the strategic capacity-choice game, building on @hackbarth2012corporate for the investment-financing framework. The Leland default framework is most natural for public-debt issuers; for the VC-backed archetypes in the calibration, "default" should be interpreted broadly as financial distress (failed funding round, liquidity crisis), consistent with @gornall2020squaring on the gap between VC valuations and the underlying economics of startup financing.

**AI economics and scaling laws.**
AI training exhibits power-law scaling [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training], motivating the concave production function; @jones1995rdbased and @bloom2020ideas study diminishing returns in idea production. @agrawal2019economics provide a comprehensive framework for AI as a prediction technology, connecting inference demand to economic value creation. On the training-inference allocation, @akcigit2018growth study exploitation versus exploration R\&D---the closest analog, but in a multi-product firm rather than a compute allocation setting.^[@berk1999optimal develop growth option decompositions that motivate the scale-gap diagnostic in @sec-valuation, which is a comparative-statics normalization rather than a growth-option decomposition. @katz1986technology and @farrell1986installed study technology adoption with network externalities and installed-base inertia. @babina2024artificial and @eisfeldt2024generative provide empirical context on AI investment and valuations; these papers could in principle discipline certain calibration inputs (e.g., AI firm betas, investment intensities), though the rapidly evolving nature of the sector limits the stability of such estimates.] On the macroeconomics of AI, @aghion2019artificial, @acemoglu2024simple, @korinek2024scenarios, and @jones2024agi analyze growth implications of transformative AI in general equilibrium; the Baumol mechanism in @aghion2019artificial, under which growth is limited by the tasks that remain essential and hard to automate, is the aggregate counterpart of the diminishing returns $\alpha < 1$ imposed at the firm level here. The present paper is partial equilibrium---it takes the demand process and discount rate as given---and therefore complements these general equilibrium analyses by providing a micro-founded model of the firm-level investment and allocation decisions that aggregate into the industry dynamics these papers study.^[@novymarx2007operating shows that operating leverage amplifies systematic risk, relevant to the operating cost parameter $\delta$.]

**Marginal contribution.**
Each building block above exists in isolation; what is new is their combination around a single margin, the *training-inference allocation under regime-specific competition with endogenous default*: the firm's choice of how to split capacity between current revenue generation and future capability building, where (a) the relevant competitive variable switches across regimes (inference capacity today, training quality tomorrow), (b) the allocation determines competitive position differently across regimes, and (c) the allocation affects firm survival through the continuation-value channel in the default boundary. This mechanism produces two results: a *faith-based survival* condition (@eq-phi-underbar) in which training investment lowers the default boundary by raising the expected post-AGI continuation value, and an asymmetric *Dario's dilemma* in which the training channel makes conservative underinvestment costlier in expected value than aggressive overinvestment of the same magnitude, while leverage concentrates the tail (default) risk on the aggressive side. Both turn on the allocation margin, and each adjacent literature is missing one of the ingredients that make it operative: the models that combine capacity choice with endogenous default [@hackbarth2014capital; @kumar2018optimal] treat installed capital as homogeneous, so there is no split to choose; the regime-switching credit models [@hackbarth2006capital; @chen2010macroeconomic; @bhamra2010levered] take the cash-flow process---and with it the size of the growth option---as exogenous, so the firm cannot buy survival by sacrificing current revenue; and the allocation problems closest in structure [@akcigit2018growth; @chod2005resource] are solved for firms whose survival is not at stake. The contribution is the joint presence of the three, not any one of them.
